sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Let's explore how to control who can access parts of your code! Visibility modifiers are like security guards for your classes.

• What `public`, `private`, and other modifiers do
• How to protect your data with encapsulation
• When to use each modifier for clean, safe code

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine your class is a house:
- `public` is like the front door - anyone can come in
- `private` is like your bedroom - only you can access it
- `protected` is like a family room - only family (subclasses) can enter

Visibility modifiers control who can see and use your class members (variables and methods).

• **Public**: Accessible from anywhere (even other packages)
  - Use for: Methods that need to be called externally
  - Example: `public void startEngine() {}`

• **Private**: Only accessible within the same class
  - Use for: Internal implementation details
  - Example: `private int fuelLevel;`

• **Protected**: Accessible within package + subclasses
  - Use for: Inheritance scenarios
  - Example: `protected String familySecret;`

• **Default (no modifier)**: Package-private (same package only)
  - Use for: Internal package organization

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ Always make fields `private` and provide controlled access via methods

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Use `private` for all instance variables by default
Provide public getters/setters only when needed
donts: Don't make everything public - it breaks encapsulation
Don't use default access unless you mean to
Don't forget to add access modifiers (default is package-private)
sections.protip: Start with the most restrictive modifier (`private`) and only open up access when necessary - it's easier to relax restrictions later than to tighten them!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is Visibility Modifiers used in real apps?

examples.how: Private fields protect sensitive data like account balances, with public methods for controlled access (deposit/withdraw)
Protected methods allow game entities to share behavior with subclasses while hiding implementation details
Public methods define the app's interface with the system, while private methods handle internal logic

problem.description:
Create a `Student` class with proper encapsulation:
1. Make all fields private
2. Provide public getters for all fields
3. Provide a public setter only for the grade (with validation)
4. Make the constructor public
hints: Fields should include: name, id, grade
Use if-statement in the grade setter for validation
problem.explanation: This solution properly encapsulates the student data by making fields private and providing controlled access. The grade setter includes validation to ensure data integrity.

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Visibility modifiers control who can access your class members
📌 Always start with the most restrictive modifier possible
📌 Practice encapsulation by hiding data and exposing controlled access
📌 You're now ready to design safer, more maintainable classes!
